```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.8,
                      dev = "png", dpi = 96)
library(lcamate)
ext <- function(...) system.file("extdata", ..., package = "lcamate")
short <- function(x, n = 48) ifelse(nchar(x) > n, paste0(substr(x, 1, n - 1), "…"), x)
```

## 1. Aim and scope

`lcamate` computes life cycle assessment (LCA) results with the matrix method of
ISO 14044 and is designed so that its results can be checked against other
engines. This vignette follows one open data source, the U.S. Life Cycle
Inventory Database (USLCI), from the raw openLCA JSON-LD export to validated
impact scores, and then shows the uncertainty and comparison tools of the
package.

Two things are kept separate throughout:

* **What is measured here**: numerical agreement with openLCA and Brightway,
  computed when this vignette is built.
* **What is assumed**: the interpretation of the database (unit conversion,
  link rules) and the impact method. Agreement with another engine validates
  the solver, not the interpretation of the data.

All files used below ship with the package (`inst/extdata`), so every number
can be reproduced.

## 2. Reading a USLCI export and checking link quality

A JSON-LD export of USLCI is a collection of processes whose technosphere inputs
point to a default provider. `read_uslci()` reads the folders `processes/` and
`flows/` and builds a model in *cut-off mode*: inputs without a valid provider
inside the database are not followed, and each process records how complete its
linking is. The package includes a miniature export of seven processes
(one of them reduced in size) that exercises every rule.

```{r mini}
m_mini <- read_uslci(ext("uslci_mini"))
m_mini
str(m_mini$report)
```

The `report` counts what the reader had to decide:

* `r1_reclassified`: land transformation/occupation inputs typed as products but
  without any producer (rule R1: treated as resource flows);
* `r2_refused`: default-provider links that point to a process whose reference
  flow is *not* the flow being consumed (rule R2: link refused);
* `skipped_unit` and `skipped_property`: exchanges that could not be converted.

Why R2 matters: in the complete 1.2026-03.0 export we analysed (1,341
processes), 219 default-provider links pointed to a process producing a
different flow (for example gasoline consumed, diesel supplied), about 5% of
the provider links. In the earlier 1.2025-06.0 export (962 processes), keeping
such links made the technosphere matrix non-productive (spectral radius of the
consumption matrix 11.3, with negative supplies), and refusing them gave a
productive system (spectral radius 0.65). These figures come from our analysis
of the full exports; they are quoted here, not recomputed by the vignette.

The completeness of each process is the share of its technosphere inputs that
are linked:

```{r completeness}
info <- m_mini$info
info$name <- short(info$name, 40)
info[order(info$completeness), c("name", "n_tech", "n_linked", "completeness")]
```

A completeness below 1 means that part of the supply chain is cut off, so the
score of that process is a **lower bound**, not a result to report. In the full
export, only 27 of 1,341 processes are closed without any external library;
all 27 are leaf processes without technosphere inputs. Chains such as electric
trucks depend on the separate *eLCI electricity baseline* library that the JSON-LD
only references. This is a property of the data distribution, not of the
package.

## 3. A validated subgraph

To exercise the solver on real chains, the package ships the closure of twelve
USLCI processes together with the eLCI electricity library: 583 processes,
restricted to the elementary flows that have a GWP100 factor. These twelve were
also calculated with the openLCA engine (olca-core 2.6.2) on the full
databases.

```{r subgraph}
procs <- read.csv(ext("uslci_subgraph_processes.csv"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
m <- read_lca_csv(ext("uslci_subgraph_exchanges.csv"), ext("uslci_subgraph_cf.csv"),
                  processes = procs$process)
m
labels <- setNames(procs$name, procs$process)
```

### 3.1 Agreement with openLCA

```{r olca}
ref <- read.csv(ext("uslci_subgraph_openlca_gwp.csv"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
scores <- lca_scores(m, "GWP100")
cmp <- data.frame(
  process = short(ref$name, 55),
  lcamate = unname(scores[ref$pid]),
  openLCA = ref$gwp_olca)
rel <- abs(cmp$lcamate - cmp$openLCA) / abs(cmp$openLCA)
cmp$rel_diff <- formatC(rel, format = "e", digits = 1)
knitr::kable(cmp, digits = c(NA, 8, 8, NA), format.args = list(scientific = FALSE),
             caption = "GWP100 per unit of reference flow (kg CO2-eq, simplified method).")
```

The largest relative difference is `r format(max(rel), digits = 2)`.
Reading the result requires three caveats that we state rather than hide:

1. Nine of the twelve processes are electric trucks; the others are two leaf
   processes (an effluent release and corn decomposition) and one extrusion
   process. The comparison covers few process types.
2. The GWP100 used here is a **simplified** method (IPCC AR5 values for 14 gases
   and CO$_2$ uptake as -1). It is meant to validate the engine, not for
   reporting. Use a full impact method for real studies.
3. Both engines read the same data. Agreement shows that the matrix algebra and
   the inventories coincide, not that the data were interpreted correctly.

### 3.2 Contributions

```{r contrib}
pid <- ref$pid[grepl("Extrusion", ref$name)][1]
res <- lca_calc(m, setNames(1, pid), "GWP100")
res$score
lca_contrib(res, n = 5, labels = setNames(short(procs$name, 50), procs$process))
```

```{r contrib-plot}
plot_contributions(res, n = 6, labels = setNames(short(procs$name, 50), procs$process))
```

Contributions are exact: they sum to the score. Every bar carries its value and
share, so the figure can be read without estimating from the axis.

### 3.3 Scores of all processes at once

`lca_scores()` solves one sparse system for the unit score of every process.
Each score is per unit of the process's own reference flow (MJ, kg, item, ...),
so scores are only comparable between processes with the same unit. As an
example, the electricity consumption mixes of the eLCI library (all per MJ):

```{r allscores}
s <- lca_scores(m, "GWP100")
mix <- grepl("^Electricity; at grid; consumption mix", labels[names(s)])
s <- sort(s[mix], decreasing = TRUE)
head(data.frame(process = unname(short(labels[names(s)], 60)), GWP100_per_MJ = unname(s)), 5)
```

## 4. Agreement with Brightway on a small database

The USLCI comparison above is with openLCA. For Brightway we use a small
database (seven processes, three flows) in which the same exchanges were loaded
in Brightway and in `lcamate`, with deterministic results saved in the package.

```{r brightway}
ex <- read.csv(ext("toy_exchanges.csv")); cf <- read.csv(ext("toy_cf.csv"))
mt <- lca_model(ex, cf)
det <- read.csv(ext("toy_brightway_det.csv"))
mats <- lca_matrices(mt)
d <- unique(det$demand)
rel <- vapply(d, function(x) {
  r <- lca_calc(mt, setNames(as.numeric(sub("^.*x", "", x)), sub("x[0-9]+$", "", x)), "GWP100", mats)
  b <- det$value[det$demand == x & det$quantity == "GWP100"]
  abs(r$score - b) / abs(b)
}, 0)
data.frame(n_demands = length(d), max_relative_difference = max(rel))
```

Differences of this size are consistent with Brightway storing characterization
factors in single precision; we have not isolated that cause separately here.

## 5. Uncertainty: independent draws, error and number of iterations

`lca_mc()` samples every exchange with a lognormal distribution (`utype == 2`)
independently, in the same way for all impact methods, and returns the scores.
`lca_mc_error()` reports the Monte Carlo error of the mean and the number of
iterations needed for a target relative error.

### 5.1 Uncertainty carried by USLCI itself

`read_uslci()` imports the uncertainty distributions that USLCI exchanges carry
(lognormal, triangular and uniform) and counts what it found in
`report$uncertainty`. Distributions that cannot be used (for example a
triangular distribution whose mode lies outside its range, or a lognormal with
a non-positive median) are counted as `unsupported` and left fixed. The package
ships seven processes that contain one case of each kind:

```{r unc-read}
m_unc <- read_uslci(ext("uslci_unc"))
str(m_unc$report$uncertainty)
```

This should be read with caution. In the complete USLCI export of version
1.2026-03.0 (77,986 exchanges in 5,651 processes) only 492 exchanges carry a
distribution with an actual spread, and 5,117 of 5,129 lognormal entries have a
geometric standard deviation of exactly 1, that is, no spread at all. A Monte
Carlo run on USLCI therefore propagates *the uncertainty that is documented*,
which is a small part of the total. To make this visible, the package reports a
coverage indicator and warns when it is low:

```{r unc-cov}
# The fixture has no climate-relevant flows, so an illustrative method is used:
# the mass of all elementary flows (every factor equal to 1).
m_unc$C <- list(emitted_mass = setNames(rep(1, length(m_unc$flows)), m_unc$flows))
p_corn <- m_unc$processes[m_unc$info$name == "Corn wet milling; operations"]
p_alum <- m_unc$processes[grepl("^Potassium sulphate", m_unc$info$name)]
unlist(lca_uncertainty_coverage(m_unc, setNames(1, p_corn), "emitted_mass"))
unlist(lca_uncertainty_coverage(m_unc, setNames(1, p_alum), "emitted_mass"))
```

`share_bio_contribution` is the share of the (absolute) direct elementary-flow
contributions that comes from exchanges with a varying distribution. Narrow
intervals in a result with low coverage mean *lack of information*, not low
uncertainty. `lca_mc_summary()`, `lca_compare_summary()` and
`lca_doe_effects()` repeat this figure and warn below 50%.

```{r unc-mc}
x_unc <- suppressWarnings(
  lca_mc(m_unc, setNames(1, p_alum), "emitted_mass", n = 500, seed = 1))
lca_mc_summary(x_unc)
```

### 5.2 Independent draws, error and number of iterations on the toy database

The functions work in the same way on any model. We use the small database
with lognormal uncertainty to illustrate error and sensitivity.

```{r mc}
x <- lca_mc(mt, c(product = 1), "GWP100", n = 500, seed = 1, keep_draws = TRUE)
lca_mc_summary(x)
lca_mc_error(unclass(x)[, 1], target_rel = 0.01)[c("n", "rel_se", "n_needed")]
```

The vignettes use a few hundred iterations to stay fast; for reported results use the `n_needed` above or more.

```{r mc-plot}
plot_mc(x)
```

The summary reports effect sizes and intervals, not p-values. With simulated
draws, a p-value only reflects the number of iterations: as Heijungs (2020)
shows, a large number of runs can lead to rejecting hypotheses that should not be rejected. How many runs
are enough for the *estimate* is a different question, answered by
`lca_mc_error()`.

`lca_sens()` screens which uncertain exchanges drive the result by Spearman
rank correlation. It is a screening measure, not a variance decomposition.

```{r sens}
lca_sens(x, top = 4)
```

## 6. Comparing two alternatives

`lca_compare()` evaluates both alternatives on the *same* sampled matrices in
every iteration, so uncertainty in what they share cancels in the difference.

```{r compare}
paired   <- lca_compare(mt, c(product = 1), c(product = 1.1), "GWP100", n = 500, seed = 1)
unpaired <- lca_compare(mt, c(product = 1), c(product = 1.1), "GWP100", n = 500, seed = 1,
                        paired = FALSE)
rbind(paired = lca_compare_summary(paired), unpaired = lca_compare_summary(unpaired))[
  , c("mean_diff", "diff_lower", "diff_upper", "prob_a_lower")]
```

Both estimate the same mean difference (they differ a little because the draws differ), but without pairing the interval is far wider
and the probability that A is lower falls, although B is by construction 10%
larger. This is why pairing matters when alternatives share processes.

```{r compare-plot}
plot_compare(paired)
```

## 7. Design of experiments on a model

Factors can be physical amounts or scenario choices. `lca_doe_run()` evaluates
every run with common random numbers, and `lca_doe_effects()` returns effects
with intervals and the probability that each effect is positive.

```{r doe}
design <- lca_doe_design(list(steel = c(1, 2), gas = c(1, 3)))
fun <- function(m, lv) lca_scale(lca_scale(m, "steel", "product", lv$steel),
                                 "gas", "elec", lv$gas)
run <- lca_doe_run(mt, design, fun, c(product = 1), "GWP100", n = 300, seed = 1)
eff <- lca_doe_effects(run)
eff
```

```{r doe-plot}
plot_effects(eff)
```

In this mode the interval reflects the uncertainty of the inputs, and no
p-values are given. When the responses are **measured on real replicates**
(a laboratory or pilot-plant experiment whose inventory feeds the model), use
the experimental mode, where the effects are fitted by least squares and
confidence intervals and p-values are meaningful. The following uses synthetic
responses only to show the interface:

```{r doe-exp}
d2 <- lca_doe_design(list(A = c(0, 1), B = c(0, 1)), replicates = 3)
set.seed(7)
X <- attr(d2, "coded")
y <- 10 + 2 * X[, "A"] + rnorm(nrow(X), sd = 0.3)   # synthetic, not data
lca_doe_effects(d2, y)
```

For fractional designs, `lca_doe_aliases()` shows which effects are confounded.

## 8. Other impact methods

The built-in GWP100 is a convenience. `lca_method_gwp()` adds a GWP100 from the
IPCC AR5 or AR6 tables by matching flow names; only gases whose values could be
checked against the report are included, and others can be added with `extra`.

```{r gwp}
mg <- lca_method_gwp(m_mini, "AR6", ch4 = "fossil")
mg$method_report[, c("category", "n_flows_matched", "share_flows_matched")]
```

For complete methods, `read_olca_method()` reads an impact method published in
openLCA JSON-LD format (for example TRACI or ReCiPe from the U.S. EPA) and
links its factors to the flows of the model **by identifier**. The package does
not distribute any method; you download the files and respect their license.
The package includes a tiny method with *invented* factors, only to show the
mechanism:

```{r method}
mm <- read_olca_method(ext("olca_method_mini"), m_mini, method = "method A")
mm$method_report[, c("category", "n_factors", "n_flows_matched", "skipped_formula",
                     "skipped_unit", "skipped_property")]
```

The report says what could not be applied: factors given only as formulas, in
a unit that is not known, or for a flow property different from the reference
property of the flow. Read `share_flows_matched` before interpreting a score:
a method that characterises few of the flows of the model says nothing about
the rest. These invented factors must not be used for any result.

### TRACI

The U.S. EPA publishes TRACI in two forms. **TRACI 2.1** comes as an openLCA
JSON-LD export linked by flow identifier and is read with `read_olca_method()`.
**TRACI 2.2** is a spreadsheet organised by substance (CAS number), and
`read_traci()` reads it:

```{r traci22, eval = FALSE}
m <- read_uslci("path/to/uslci")                # keeps the CAS number of each flow
m <- read_traci("path/to/TRACI_2_2.xlsx", m)    # needs the readxl package
m$method_report                                 # factors and flows matched per category
m$traci_report                                  # matches by CAS and by name
```

In the USLCI export, about a third of the elementary flows used by the processes are
missing from the flow folder, so they carry no CAS number (this includes "Carbon dioxide"
emitted to air). `read_traci()` therefore compares flows without a CAS with the TRACI
substance names (exact, case-insensitive); without this step, the TRACI global warming
of most processes was far below the built-in GWP100.

Three things to keep in mind. First, the 2.2 workbook has no eutrophication and
no fossil-fuel depletion (the EPA removed them in 2022). Second, ecotoxicity and
human-health factors depend on the emission compartment, and mapping the category
path of each flow to a TRACI compartment is an **assumption** (documented in
`?read_traci` and overridable). Third, TRACI global warming is based on IPCC AR4,
so it will differ from `lca_method_gwp()`.

### Checking the input data

`lca_check()` looks for problems that do not stop the calculation but change the
result silently: repeated rows, elementary flows that no method characterises,
processes without data, inconsistent uncertainty parameters, flows without a CAS
number and names that differ by one character. It also asks whether the system can
be solved at all (self-consumption, unproductive cycles, singular or badly conditioned
matrices) and, when the exchanges have a `unit` column, whether a flow appears in
different units. It lists what it did **not** check. The USLCI exchanges carry no
unit column because `read_uslci()` already converts every amount to the reference
unit of its unit group.

```{r check, eval = FALSE}
lca_check(m)
lca_check(m, demand = c("my process id" = 1), method = "Global warming")
```

## 9. Limitations

* The impact method in the examples is a simplified GWP100; full methods are
  read from files you provide (`read_olca_method()`), and the reader has been
  tested only with invented test factors until real files are validated.
* USLCI documents very little uncertainty (0.6% of the exchanges of the full
  export carry a varying distribution); intervals from Monte Carlo on USLCI
  data are lower bounds of the real uncertainty. Pedigree-derived uncertainty
  is not applied.
* The reader does not read the openLCA library format yet; library processes
  enter through the precomputed subgraph.
* The validation against openLCA covers twelve processes (nine of them electric
  trucks), and the validation against Brightway a seven-process database.
* USLCI describes United States systems.
* The conclusions about the link rules (R1, R2) come from the analysis of one
  database version.

```{r session}
sessionInfo()
```

**Data.** U.S. Life Cycle Inventory Database (NREL/USLCI, MIT license); see
